prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, cancer, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but they suspect that some of their costs may be out of whack.
prompt.question: Is it true that some of Vitality's costs are out of whack, and if so, what should they do about it?

clarifying_info.q: Who are Vitality's competitors and how is the market?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has a few competitors who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the leader in the space. Competition is not the focus. The market is mature.

clarifying_info.q: How large is Vitality's sales force and how are agents compensated?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has over 10,000 field sales agents who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium, defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other incentive mechanisms beyond the base commission?
clarifying_info.a: In addition to the commission, short-term priorities are often communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
clarifying_info.a: Major costs are sales, G&A (General and Administrative), and advertising.

clarifying_info.q: What is the agent turnover situation?
clarifying_info.a: Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Results and Major Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key financial results and cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in $000s).

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process and Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A table showing the number of agent-focused sales contests targeted at each stage of the selling process (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Gain active policyholders, Keep accounts active, Produce results/Premium, Reactivating dormant account) for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

exhibits.title: Snapshot of 'Sweeps Week' Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing weekly premium as a ratio to the average weekly premium (2008-2010 baseline = 100%) for weeks 1-27 (January through June) across years 2008, 2009, and 2010. Two 'Sweeps Week' contests in 2010 are marked at weeks 4 and 20.

data.y_axis: Ratio to Average Weekly Premium (2008-2010), 0% to 200%
data.pattern: Weeks immediately surrounding each Sweeps Week show depressed premium relative to the 2008/2009 baselines

framework: Diagnose cost structure: compare all cost lines year-over-year to identify which cost(s) are growing abnormally relative to premium/revenue growth
Quantify the anomaly: calculate growth rates for each cost line and compare against premium growth (should be ~10% p.a.)
Understand root cause: investigate the selling process and incentive structure — specifically any changes to the sales contest mix in 2010
Evaluate effectiveness: determine whether the incremental sales cost generated proportional incremental premium and profit
Recommend action: eliminate ineffective contests and redirect spending toward activities not duplicated by the base commission structure

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What do you observe about the cost structure and profitability trends from 2008 to 2010?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates should: (1) note that G&A and advertising grow at roughly 10% per year, consistent with premium growth; (2) spot that sales costs grow 10% from 2008-2009 (250→275) but jump 45% from 2009-2010 (275→400), far outpacing 10% premium growth; (3) note that profit margins decline from 9.5% to 9.4% to 8.5%, suggesting the extra sales spend is NOT generating proportional revenue. The key insight is that sales costs are the sole anomaly.

math.setup: Calculate YoY growth rates for each cost line and compare against premium growth rate of 10%.
steps: G&A growth 2009-2010: (58-55)/55 ≈ 5.5% (slightly below 10%, broadly in line)
Sales cost growth 2009-2010: (400-275)/275 = 45.5% — ABNORMAL vs. 10% premium growth
Profit margin 2010 check: approximate profit = 3,025,000 × 8.5% ≈ $257,125 vs. 2009: 2,750,000 × 9.4% ≈ $258,500 — profit essentially flat despite 10% revenue growth
math.answer: Sales costs grew 45% in 2010 vs. 10% premium growth — they are the only cost out of whack. Profit margins are declining, meaning the extra sales spend is not paying off.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 2. What changed in Vitality's sales contest mix in 2010 compared to prior years, and what does this tell you?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify the structural shift: (1) contests targeting 'Gain active policyholders' dropped from 4 to 0; (2) contests on 'Reactivating dormant accounts' dropped from 2 to 0; (3) contests targeting 'Acquire new accounts' doubled from 2 to 4; (4) contests targeting 'Produce results (Premium)' doubled from 2 to 4. This means in 2010 Vitality shifted focus toward new account acquisition and total premium — both of which are more expensive and partially duplicative of the base commission structure. Strong candidates will note that acquiring new customers costs considerably more than retaining or up-selling existing ones, which would further compress margins.

questions.prompt: You are told that one of the new 2010 premium-focused contests was called 'Sweeps Week': Vitality paid an extra 10% commission on all premium booked during two designated low-volume weeks. Look at Exhibit 3. Was 'Sweeps Week' effective?
questions.guidance: The candidate should read the chart correctly: the two Sweeps Week contests (weeks 4 and 20) show dramatic spikes to ~200% of average premium in those specific weeks. However, the weeks immediately before and after each Sweeps Week show depressed premium relative to both the 2010 trend and the 2008/2009 baselines. This indicates agents 'gamed' the system by pulling forward or pushing back sales to land in the Sweeps Week window and earn the extra 10% commission. Net new premium generated was likely minimal — the contest merely shifted timing, not total volume. Furthermore, the contest's focus on driving premium was already covered by the base commission structure, making it duplicative and wasteful.

math.setup: Conceptual — net incremental premium from Sweeps Week is approximately zero because adjacent weeks are depressed by roughly the same amount as the spike.
steps: Week 4 spike: ~200% of average = roughly +100% above baseline for that week
Adjacent weeks (e.g., weeks 3 and 5) in 2010 are visibly below the 2008/2009 baseline
Inference: total premium over the Jan-Jun period for 2010 is not materially higher than prior years despite two Sweeps Weeks — agents shifted timing, not total output
math.answer: Sweeps Week was not effective. It generated no net incremental premium; it only redistributed existing sales across weeks. Vitality paid an extra 10% commission on premium that would have been booked anyway.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond eliminating 'Sweeps Week', what other actions could Vitality take to improve profitability through its sales contest and incentive structure?

categories.name: Redesign contest objectives
ideas: Shift contests back to activities NOT covered by base commission (e.g., reactivating dormant accounts, gaining active policyholders)
Introduce contests targeting cross-sell or up-sell depth within existing accounts
Design contests around agent retention/productivity rather than raw premium

categories.name: Improve contest mechanics
ideas: Use cumulative targets rather than single-week spikes to prevent gaming
Cap the incremental commission to limit cost exposure
Use rank-based prizes rather than per-unit incremental commissions

categories.name: Evaluate new account focus
ideas: Analyze LTV of new accounts vs. incremental cost of acquisition before keeping the new-account contest increase
Assess whether there is a strategic rationale (e.g., entering new employer markets) justifying the new account push
Compare CAC against expected premium stream from new accounts

categories.name: Address agent behavior
ideas: Implement guardrails on enrollment timing manipulation (e.g., require enrollment within 48 hours of application)
Increase transparency by sharing gaming data with field managers
Adjust commission settlement rules to discourage timing manipulation

recommendation: Eliminate the 'Sweeps Week' contest for 2011. The contest drove no net new premium — agents gamed it by shifting sales timing — while costing Vitality an extra 10% commission on premium that would have been booked regardless. This is the primary driver of the abnormal 45% increase in sales costs in 2010.

Repurpose the freed contest budget toward activities not already incentivized by the base commission structure, such as reactivating dormant accounts or deepening policyholder engagement, which were abandoned in the 2010 contest mix.

Investigate the four new-account focused contests added in 2010 before eliminating them. If there is a deliberate strategic rationale for expanding the customer base, the cost may be justified — but this requires a full LTV vs. CAC analysis. If not strategic, reduce these contests as well.
risks: If agents have become accustomed to 'Sweeps Week' earnings, eliminating it may reduce morale or increase turnover — particularly risky given already high agent attrition.
Shifting contest focus away from premium may cause a short-term dip in reported premium if agents disengage; must manage the transition carefully.
Without data on the two other new-account contests, we cannot fully assess whether removing them would harm a legitimate strategic initiative.
next_steps: Conduct a detailed LTV vs. CAC analysis on the 2010 new account cohort to evaluate whether the new-account contest investment was justified.
Interview top-performing field managers to understand how Sweeps Week influenced agent behavior and test the gaming hypothesis with transaction-level data.
Design a replacement contest focused on dormant account reactivation or cross-sell, pilot in one region before national rollout.
Establish a monitoring framework tracking sales cost as a percentage of new premium on a monthly basis to detect future anomalies early.
